title: Discourse on Inequality
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
openingChapterLabel: Dedication — To the Republic of Geneva
openingText: MOST HONORABLE, MAGNIFICENT AND SOVEREIGN LORDS: convinced that only a virtuous citizen can offer his country honors it can rightfully accept, I have spent thirty years trying to make myself worthy of paying you some public tribute. Since this fortunate occasion partly makes up for what my efforts could not, I have allowed myself to consult here the zeal that moves me rather than the standing that should authorize me. Having had the good fortune to be born among you, how could I reflect on the equality nature established between human beings, and the inequality they themselves have introduced, without also reflecting on the deep wisdom by which both are combined in your state in the manner most in keeping with natural law, most favorable to society, to public order, and to individual happiness? In searching for the best rules common sense can lay down for the constitution of a government, I have been so struck to find them all already in force in yours that, even had I not been born within your walls, I would have felt it my duty to offer this portrait of human society to that people which, more than any other, seems to possess its greatest advantages and to have best guarded against its abuses.
about:
Where do differences in wealth, power, and esteem come from? Rousseau distinguishes natural differences, such as age and strength, from moral or political inequality created through human conventions and institutions. He asks how property, the division of labor, and dependence enlarge those differences.

Published in 1755, the work here comprises a dedication to Geneva, a preface, and two main parts. The first examines a hypothetical human being before social life; the second follows developments toward property, government, and arbitrary power. Rousseau presents conjectural reasoning rather than a documented history of humanity.

angleCards.title: What is natural?
angleCards.text: Rousseau separates what humans owe to nature from what life among others has made them. Follow the assumptions behind his original human being.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine what the state of nature explains and which assumptions that explanation needs.

angleCards.title: Property and dependence
angleCards.text: Land, divided labor, and shared rules change human relationships. Watch the intervening steps that connect possession to political power.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the argument from property and labor to laws, government, and oppression.

angleCards.title: Compassion and comparative self-love
angleCards.text: Rousseau distinguishes self-preservation from the self-love that depends on comparison with others. Compassion plays a separate role.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand amour de soi and amour-propre and examine the role of compassion.

angleCards.title: Who benefits from progress?
angleCards.text: Greater skills and wealth can bring new needs and dependence. Rousseau asks what development means for freedom and happiness.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test the critique of progress without assuming that every change must mean decline.

cast.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
cast.description: He dedicates the work to the Republic of Geneva and examines inequality through a conjectural account of human development, connecting human feelings with social arrangements.

cast.name: Natural man
cast.description: A hypothetical human with few needs and few ties to others, used to examine which capacities require a developed society.

cast.name: Amour-propre
cast.description: A feeling dependent on comparison and the judgment of others, distinguished from the natural self-love directed toward self-preservation.

cast.name: Property
cast.description: Property rights help explain the division between rich and poor and the institutions that subsequently make inequality secure.

cast.name: The Academy of Dijon
cast.description: The work answers the academy’s question about the origin of inequality and whether natural law authorizes it. Rousseau therefore distinguishes its emergence from its justification.

whyItMatters.title: Explaining inequality
whyItMatters.body: Rousseau examines how social arrangements make differences durable and give them legal protection. The reader is invited to distinguish a difference’s origin from its justification.

whyItMatters.title: Freedom and dependence
whyItMatters.body: Cooperation can develop human abilities while increasing dependence. The work asks how that dependence becomes domination and how a government intended to protect freedom can end up destroying it.

whyItMatters.title: Living through others’ judgments
whyItMatters.body: The conclusion portrays people whose sense of their own worth depends on others’ opinions. It makes esteem, competition, and personal satisfaction central questions for the reader.
